title: Mesha and the world of Moab
draftNote: First research draft, step 2 of the next twenty study drafts, written 2026-11-05. Its scope was widened the same day, after the site's redundancy review, from the Mesha Stele alone to Israel's three neighbour kingdoms east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea, Moab, Ammon and Edom, with the stele as the anchor. The stele's own record, and its comparison with 2 Kings 3, are already in From discovery to history and Israel among the empires; this draft links them and does not repeat them. The landing at /study/mesha-and-the-world-of-moab keeps its title and artwork and is not touched. No page, route or component. Several sources were read through a tool that returns a report on a web page and short quoted phrases, not the page itself; each such source says so, and its quotations are to be checked before a page is built.
premise: Across the Jordan and the Dead Sea from Israel lay three small kingdoms, Moab, Ammon and Edom, which Scripture traces to Lot and to Esau and calls Israel's kin, and which fought, traded, married and were judged beside Israel for a thousand years. One of their kings, Mesha of Moab, left the longest inscription any of them has given us, and around it stand a few Ammonite and Edomite finds that let the three speak, briefly, in their own words.
question: When Israel's neighbours speak for themselves, what do they add to Scripture's account of them, and what do they leave to Scripture alone?
outcomes: Place Moab, Ammon and Edom on the land: their rivers and borders, their chief cities, and the road that ran through all three.
Name each kingdom's god, Chemosh, Milcom and Qos, and say where each is known from: Scripture, the neighbours' own inscriptions and names, or both.
Set the kings Scripture names beside the kings the inscriptions and the Assyrian records name, and say which appear in both and which in only one.
Follow the three through Scripture, from Lot's sons and Esau to Herod's family, and say what the prophets charge each with and what they promise.

boundaries.in: The three kingdoms east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea, together: their land and roads, their gods, their kings in Scripture and in inscriptions, the finds that carry their own words (the Mesha Stele as anchor, the Amman Citadel inscription, the Tell Siran bottle, seal impressions naming kings and servants, Bozrah and the copper works of Faynan), the stories that tie them to Israel from Genesis 19 to the prophets, and the Idumeans of New Testament times, Herod's people. The "house of David" reading on the stele, briefly, with both sides named.
out: The Mesha Stele as an object (its finding at Dhiban in 1868, its breaking, the paper squeeze, its Louvre record) and the comparison of its account with 2 Kings 3: From discovery to history holds both, with their sources. Section 01 here is a short pointer.
Mesha's place among the empires, beside Qarqar, Jehu and Assyria: Israel among the empires.
The full argument over line 31 of the stele, letter by letter: From discovery to history. Section 01 here names the two readings and who holds each.
Edom's later neighbours to the south, the Nabataeans and Petra, except where they bear on the Idumeans.

Herod the Great's reign, buildings and family as rulers: The world of Jesus & the apostles and the draft study Rulers and their choices. Section 09 here is about one thing only, where the Idumeans came from.
The prophets as prophets, in their own setting: the draft study Prophets in their times. Here their oracles are read only for what they say of the three neighbours.
Ruth's book as a story of faith and kindness: Ruth is read here for one fact, that David's great-grandmother was a Moabite.

stele.head: The stele, briefly
stele.evidence: The Mesha Stele (Louvre AO 5066) is a basalt monument found at Dhiban, ancient Dibon, in 1868, broken before it could be moved, and pieced together from fragments and a paper squeeze made before the breaking. Its 34 lines, in Moabite, give Mesha's own account of how Moab came out from under Omri's house, and of the towns he took and built. Scripture's account is 2 Kings 1:1 and 3:4-27: "Now Mesha king of Moab was a sheep breeder" (2 Kings 3:4 · BSB), who paid Israel tribute and "after the death of Ahab ... rebelled against the king of Israel" (2 Kings 3:5 · BSB).
stele.inference: Two witnesses tell of one rebellion from opposite sides, and neither is a copy of the other. That comparison is the subject of From discovery to history, and is not repeated here. This study uses the stele for something else: it is the one long text in which any of Israel's three eastern neighbours describes its own land, its own god and its own king.
stele.limit: The stele's record, its date range and its sources are in From discovery to history and Israel among the empires. The date of finding is taken from From discovery to history; the count of 34 lines is the usual one, as published translations number them.

lines.head: Moab in its own words
lines.lead: Four lines of the stele, in K. C. Hanson's English, adapted from W. F. Albright. Hanson spells the god Kemosh; this study writes Chemosh, as the Berean does.

items.quote: I am Mesha, son of Kemosh[-yatti], the king of Moab, the Dhibanite.
items.note: A king, his father, his land and his town. The brackets mark letters restored. The father's name is usually completed from a fragment found at Kerak in 1958 (Jordan Archaeological Museum 6807), which names a Chemosh-yat; that he is Mesha's father is an inference.

items.quote: Omri was the king of Israel, and he oppressed Moab for many days, for Kemosh was angry with his land.
items.note: Defeat explained as the god's anger, as Judges explains Eglon's rule over Israel as the LORD's doing.

items.quote: And the men of Gad lived in the land of Atarot from ancient times; and the king of Israel built Atarot for himself, and I fought against the city and captured it.
items.note: Mesha agrees with Numbers that Gad lived at Ataroth. An altar with two Moabite inscriptions was found in the Moabite sanctuary at Khirbat Ataruz in 2010 (section 05).

items.quote: And from there I took Yahweh's vessels, and I presented them before Kemosh's face.
items.note: The earliest certain mention of the LORD's name outside the Bible, in an enemy's boast. Before this, Mesha says Chemosh told him to take Nebo from Israel.

items.quote: I have built Aroer, and I constructed the military road in Arnon.
items.note: The Arnon gorge, Moab's old border, crossed by the king's own road.

lines.evidence: The stele names Moab's god, its king and his father, Omri and Israel, the LORD, the tribe of Gad, and towns Scripture also names: Dibon, Medeba, Ataroth, Nebo, Jahaz and Aroer among them.
lines.inference: Moab's king and Israel's Scripture place the same people in the same towns, and both explain war by their god. The stele is the best evidence there is for how Moab saw itself.
lines.limit: The quotations are from a modern adaptation of a 1969 translation, read on Hanson's page; a page should check them against a current edition before quoting. That the stele is the earliest certain mention of the LORD's name is the usual judgment; it depends on how earlier Egyptian place names reading Yahu are taken.

davidLine.head: "House of David"? Two readings of a damaged line
davidLine.evidence: Line 31 of the stele is damaged. In 1994 André Lemaire proposed that it reads "house of David", which would make the stele, with the Tel Dan inscription, one of the earliest texts outside the Bible to name David's dynasty.

views.who: For the reading: André Lemaire (1994, and with Jean-Philippe Delorme in 2023, answering critics); Michael Langlois, from new photographs in 2019, who calls it hypothetical but the most probable reading.
views.held: The traces fit the letters of "house of David", and a king of Judah suits the context of a campaign in Moab's south.

views.who: Against it: Philip R. Davies at once, in 1994; Israel Finkelstein, Nadav Na'aman and Thomas Römer (2019), who propose a three-letter name and cautiously suggest Balak, the king of Moab in Numbers 22; Matthieu Richelle and Andrew Burlingame (2023), who question several of the marks the reading depends on.
views.held: The space and the surviving marks do not support "house of David" as a secure reading.

davidLine.inference: Neither reading is visible on the stone as it stands; each is a restoration of damaged letters. The site does not need the line either way: Scripture's David does not wait on an inscription.
davidLine.limit: From discovery to history holds this argument in full, with each paper and what was read of it. This study names the two sides and goes no further.

kings.head: Two records of kings. They barely meet.
kings.lead: Scripture names the neighbours' kings in its own story. The Assyrian kings' records, and a few of the neighbours' own objects, name others. Set the two lists side by side and the pattern shows at once.

rows.name: Balak son of Zippor
rows.when: The wilderness years; no date given.
rows.note: One reading of the damaged line 31 of the Mesha Stele restores his name (section 01); it is a proposal, not a reading of visible letters.

rows.name: Mesha
rows.when: The ninth century BC, after Ahab's death.
rows.note: The one king of the three named in both records beyond doubt.

rows.name: Mesha's father, whose name begins with Chemosh
rows.outside: The stele's first line, and a fragment from Kerak
rows.note: Only the first part survives on the stele. Many restore it as Chemosh-yat from a basalt fragment found at Kerak in 1958, which names a Chemosh-yat but does not say he was Mesha's father.

rows.name: Salamanu
rows.outside: Tiglath-pileser III's tribute list (Nimrud tablet K.3751)
rows.note: Some have linked him with "Shalman" in Hosea 10:14 ("as Shalman devastated Beth-arbel", Hosea 10:14 · BSB); the identification is a guess.

rows.name: Kammusunadbi
rows.note: His name begins with Kammusu, Chemosh.

rows.name: Buduili (Budu-ilu)
rows.note: Spelled Puduil in some translations of Esarhaddon's list.

rows.name: Amminadab
rows.outside: The Tell Siran bottle, which names two kings Amminadab with Hissalel between them; an Amminadab also among Ashurbanipal's tributaries
rows.note: Not the Amminadab of Ruth 4:19, an ancestor of David; the name is shared.

rows.name: Baalis
rows.outside: Probably Ba'alyasha, on a seal impression from Tell el-Umeiri naming his servant
rows.note: The match is probable, not certain: the spellings differ, and there may have been more than one king of the name.

rows.name: Eight kings, from Bela son of Beor to Hadad
rows.when: "before any king reigned over the Israelites" (Genesis 36:31 · BSB).
rows.note: None is said to be his predecessor's son, and several are given a different home town.

rows.name: Hadad the Edomite
rows.note: "from the royal line of Edom" (1 Kings 11:14 · BSB), not said to have reigned.

rows.name: Qaus-malaka
rows.note: His name is built on Qos.

rows.name: Qaus-gabri
rows.outside: Esarhaddon's list; and a clay sealing from Umm el-Biyara at Petra reading Qos-ga[br], king of E[dom], partly restored
rows.note: His name too is built on Qos.

kings.unnamed: Scripture also has kings it does not name: the king of Moab who sheltered David's parents (1 Samuel 22:3), the king of Edom who refused Israel passage (Numbers 20:14) and the one who marched with Israel against Mesha (2 Kings 3:9), the Ammonite king whose crown David took (2 Samuel 12:30), and the kings whose envoys came to Zedekiah (Jeremiah 27:3).
kings.evidence: Of eighteen named rows, only Mesha stands in both records for certain, and Baalis probably. Scripture's named kings of the three fall almost all before 800 BC; the outside records' named kings fall almost all after 734 BC, when Assyria's lists begin to include them.
kings.inference: The two records mostly cover different centuries, which is why they so rarely meet. An outside list that lacks Eglon or Nahash does not deny them: it does not reach their time. And Scripture, which tells Israel's story and not Edom's, has no reason to name Edom's kings under Assyria.
kings.limit: The outside list is what survives and has been published, not a full king list of any of the three. Assyrian spellings vary by translation: these follow the translations named in the sources, with a second spelling where one is common.

kingdoms.lead: Three kingdoms in a row, north to south, on the high ground east of the Jordan valley, the Dead Sea and the Arabah. Rivers cut deep gorges westward across the plateau, and the gorges made the borders.

items.name: Ammon
items.land: The upper Jabbok (Wadi Zarqa) and the hills around its source, north of Moab and east of Gilead.
items.city: Rabbah, "Rabbah of the Ammonites" (2 Samuel 12:26 · BSB); today Amman, the capital of Jordan.
items.ancestor: Ben-ammi, Lot's younger daughter's son: "He is the father of the Ammonites of today" (Genesis 19:38 · BSB).
items.evidence: Numbers stops Israel's conquest of Sihon's land "up to the border of the Ammonites, because it was fortified" (Numbers 21:24 · BSB). Ammon's own finds cluster around Amman: the Citadel inscription and the Tell Siran bottle (section 05).
items.inference: Ammon was the smallest of the three in land and the closest to Israel's tribes in Gilead, and its quarrels with Israel are over that edge: Jabesh-gilead, the land "from the Arnon to the Jabbok" (Judges 11:13 · BSB), and Gad.
items.limit: Its borders are given in Scripture as Israel saw them and moved with each war. Where Ammon ended and Gilead began at any one time is not certain.

items.name: Moab
items.land: The plateau directly east of the Dead Sea. Its heartland lay between the Arnon (Wadi Mujib) and the Zered (Wadi Hasa); the tableland north of the Arnon, with Medeba, Dibon and Heshbon, was fought over with Israel.
items.city: Dibon (Dhiban), Mesha's own town, where the stele was found; and Kir-hareseth, usually identified with Kerak, the city Israel besieged in 2 Kings 3.
items.ancestor: Moab, Lot's elder daughter's son: "He is the father of the Moabites of today" (Genesis 19:37 · BSB).
items.evidence: "the Arnon is the border between the Moabites and the Amorites" (Numbers 21:13 · BSB). Israel's tribes Reuben and Gad were given the land north of it, and "the Gadites built up Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer" (Numbers 32:34 · BSB). Mesha's stele claims the same towns for Moab.
items.inference: The tableland north of the Arnon is the ground both texts care about. Moab's history with Israel is in large part the history of who held Dibon, Medeba and Ataroth.
items.limit: That Kir-hareseth is Kerak is the usual identification, not one an inscription on the site has confirmed.

items.name: Edom
items.land: South of the Zered, the highlands east of the Arabah running toward the Gulf of Aqaba, called Seir in Scripture; and below them, at the edge of the Arabah, the copper district of Faynan. Late in its history Edomites were living west of the Arabah too, in Judah's Negev.
items.city: Bozrah (Buseirah); Sela, taken by Amaziah (2 Kings 14:7); Teman, often a name for the whole land.
items.ancestor: Esau, Jacob's twin: "This is the account of Esau (that is, Edom)" (Genesis 36:1 · BSB).
items.god: Qos (section 04), a name Scripture never uses.
items.evidence: Jacob sends messengers "to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom" (Genesis 32:3 · BSB). Amos threatens fire "upon Teman to consume the citadels of Bozrah" (Amos 1:12 · BSB). Bozrah has been excavated (section 05).
items.inference: Edom is the kingdom Scripture ties most closely to Israel, by a twin brother, and the one it charges most bitterly, for what Edom did when Jerusalem fell (section 08).
items.limit: Where Sela was is argued: a rock near Buseirah and the mountain of Umm el-Biyara at Petra are both proposed. When Edom first had a king of its own is the subject of the explanations below.

roads.lead: One road joined the three, and Israel asked twice to use it.

items.name: The King's Highway
items.evidence: Moses asks the king of Edom, "We will stay on the King’s Highway; we will not turn to the right or to the left until we have passed through your territory" (Numbers 20:17 · BSB), and asks Sihon the same (Numbers 21:22). Edom answers, "You may not travel through our land" (Numbers 20:18 · BSB).
items.inference: A road along the plateau, through the kingdoms' towns, is what the request assumes. Refused, Israel goes around: "Israel traveled through the wilderness and bypassed the lands of Edom and Moab" (Judges 11:18 · BSB).
items.limit: "The King's Highway" is now the modern name of the old north-south route through Jordan's highlands, taken from these verses. Whether Numbers names one fixed road or means a royal road in general is not settled.

items.name: The Arabah road
items.evidence: Israel "turned away from the Arabah road, which comes up from Elath and Ezion-geber, and traveled along the road of the Wilderness of Moab" (Deuteronomy 2:8 · BSB).
items.inference: The valley floor south of the Dead Sea was a second way north, past the copper district of Faynan.
items.limit: Deuteronomy names the roads; it does not map them.

items.name: The way of the Desert of Edom
items.evidence: Against Mesha, Israel's king chooses to go "By way of the Desert of Edom" (2 Kings 3:8 · BSB): "a roundabout route for seven days" (2 Kings 3:9 · BSB), with Judah and Edom.
items.inference: Coming round the south end of the Dead Sea let the allies strike Moab from its weaker southern side, away from the towns Mesha had fortified in the north.
items.limit: This is a common reading of the route; the text gives the direction and the days, not the reason.

gods.lead: Each kingdom had a chief god, and Scripture names two of them as Solomon's sin. The third is known only from outside it.

items.name: Chemosh
items.scripture: Moab is "O people of Chemosh" (Numbers 21:29 · BSB). Solomon builds "a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab" (1 Kings 11:7 · BSB), and Josiah desecrates it (2 Kings 23:13). Jeremiah says "Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and officials" (Jeremiah 48:7 · BSB).
items.outside: The Mesha Stele speaks for Chemosh throughout: he is angry with his land, he speaks to Mesha, he drives Israel out. His name is part of royal names: Mesha's father's name begins with it, and Sennacherib's annals name a king of Moab, Kammusu-nadbi.
items.evidence: Scripture and Moab agree on the god's name and on his place as Moab's own god. Both explain defeat as their god's anger and victory as his gift.
items.inference: Mesha's language is close to Israel's: on the stele the people of a captured town are devoted to destruction for the god, the same practice Scripture calls being "devoted to the LORD for destruction" (Joshua 6:17 · BSB). The two peoples spoke of war in the same terms and gave the credit to different gods.
items.limit: Jephthah, speaking to the king of the Ammonites, says "your god Chemosh" (Judges 11:24 · BSB), though Chemosh was Moab's god. Readers explain this differently: the land in dispute had been Moab's, Ammon was then ruling Moab, or Jephthah was arguing in his hearer's terms. The text does not say.

items.name: Milcom, and Molech
items.scripture: Solomon follows "Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites" (1 Kings 11:5 · BSB) and builds a high place "for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites" (1 Kings 11:7 · BSB). Jeremiah asks, "Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?" (Jeremiah 49:1 · BSB). The law forbids giving children "to be sacrificed to Molech" (Leviticus 18:21 · BSB).
items.outside: Ammonite inscriptions and seals write the god's name mlkm, and Ammonite personal names are built on it. The Amman Citadel inscription probably names Milcom in its first line, if a damaged letter is rightly restored (section 05).
items.evidence: Milcom is Ammon's god both in Scripture and in Ammon's own writing. Molech is tied to Ammon once, in 1 Kings 11:7; elsewhere Molech is named with child sacrifice in the Valley of Ben-hinnom (2 Kings 23:10).
items.inference: In 1 Kings 11:7 the two names are used of one Ammonite god. Whether Molech is that god everywhere is a separate question.
items.limit: Josiah's reform lists Molech at Topheth (2 Kings 23:10) and Milcom on the hill east of Jerusalem (2 Kings 23:13) separately, and scholars divide: some take Molech as another spelling of Milcom, some as a different god, and since Otto Eissfeldt in 1935 some have argued that molk was a word for a kind of sacrifice, not a god at all (located, not read). Ammon's own inscriptions say nothing of child sacrifice. In 2 Samuel 12:30 the Berean reads "the crown from the head of their king"; the same Hebrew letters can be read as Milcom, and some translations read it so.

items.name: Qos
items.scripture: Never named. After defeating Edom, Amaziah "brought back the gods of the Seirites, set them up as his own gods" (2 Chronicles 25:14 · BSB); no name is given.
items.outside: Edomite kings' names are built on Qos: Qaus-malaku in Tiglath-pileser III's records and Qaus-gabri in Esarhaddon's. Inscriptions to Qos come from Horvat Qitmit, an Edomite shrine in the Negev. Josephus, in the first century AD, says Costobarus, an Idumean who married Herod's sister, was "one whose ancestors had been priests to the Koze" (Antiquities 15.7.9, in Whiston's translation), a name usually taken as Qos.
items.evidence: Qos is known as Edom's god from names, inscriptions and Josephus, over about seven centuries, and not from Scripture.
items.inference: Scripture's silence is not ignorance: it names the gods of Edom's neighbours and calls Edom's gods simply gods. Some scholars find Qos in the name Barkos among the temple servants who returned from exile (Ezra 2:53); that is a reading of the name, not something the text says.
items.limit: What was believed about Qos, and how he was worshipped, is hardly known. Josephus's next words, calling Koze a god of the Idumeans, were not confirmed word for word and are not quoted.

finds.head: Their own words, and their own ground
finds.lead: Beyond the Mesha Stele, a handful of objects and sites carry the neighbours' own writing or show their work. Each is given with where it is kept, what it says, and where it stops.

items.name: The Amman Citadel inscription
items.what: Eight broken lines cut in stone, found on the Citadel hill of Amman in 1961; first published by Siegfried H. Horn in 1969.
items.date: The later ninth century BC, by the shape of its letters: an estimate.
items.evidence: Ammon's longest early inscription. Its first line probably names Milcom, if a damaged letter is rightly restored.
items.inference: Ammon, like Moab, wrote royal or temple texts in its own language and credited its god.
items.limit: The text is broken on every side, and its translation differs from scholar to scholar. The reading of Milcom depends on a restored letter.

items.name: The Tell Siran bottle
items.what: A bronze bottle about 10 cm long, found in 1972 at Tell Siran, on the campus of the University of Jordan in Amman, with a short inscription cut on its side.
items.date: About 600 BC by Frank Moore Cross's dating of the letters; its first editors, Henry O. Thompson and Fawzi Zayadine, placed it earlier in the seventh century. A range.
items.evidence: It names its maker's king and his line: Amminadab, king of the Ammonites, son of Hissalel, king of the Ammonites, son of Amminadab, king of the Ammonites. The rest of the text speaks of the king's works.
items.inference: Ammon had a dynasty of at least three generations in the seventh century, unknown to Scripture.
items.limit: Its purpose, and what the bottle held, are argued. The kings' dates come from the letters' shapes and from an Assyrian mention of an Amminadab, not from the bottle.

items.name: The seal impression of Baalis's servant
items.what: A seal impression on a small clay stopper, found at Tell el-Umeiri near Amman in 1984 by the Madaba Plains Project, reading "belonging to Milkom'or, servant of Ba'alyasha'".
items.kept: Not confirmed in the sources read.
items.evidence: An Ammonite official named after Milcom served a king named Ba'alyasha.
items.inference: Ba'alyasha is probably the "Baalis king of the Ammonites" (Jeremiah 40:14 · BSB), the king who plotted Gedaliah's death.
items.limit: Probable, not certain: the spellings differ, and there may have been more than one king of the name. Published by Larry G. Herr in 1985 (located, not read).

items.name: The inscribed altar of Khirbat Ataruz
items.what: A stone altar about 50 cm high from a Moabite sanctuary at Khirbat Ataruz, ancient Ataroth, found in 2010, with two short Moabite inscriptions and Egyptian-style numerals.
items.kept: Not confirmed in the sources read.
items.date: The later ninth or early eighth century BC, by the letters: close to Mesha's time.
items.evidence: A Moabite cult place stood at the town Mesha says he took from Gad.
items.inference: Ataroth was Moabite in the generation after Mesha, as the stele says it became.
items.limit: The inscriptions are short and their reading is the editors'. Published by Adam L. Bean, Christopher A. Rollston, P. Kyle McCarter and Stefan J. Wimmer in 2018 (located through its abstract, not read).

items.name: Bozrah (Buseirah)
items.what: Edom's chief city, excavated by Crystal-M. Bennett in 1971-1974 and 1980; the final report, edited by Piotr Bienkowski, appeared in 2002.
items.kept: The site is in southern Jordan.
items.date: Settled from the late eighth century BC; its main Edomite phase runs into the sixth.
items.evidence: Large public buildings, usually described as a palace and a temple, from Edom's years under Assyria.
items.inference: Bozrah was the centre of Edom's government and worship when Amos, Isaiah and Jeremiah named it. Its report calls it the centre of a loosely organised Edom rather than the capital of a nation state.
items.limit: Nothing found there is earlier than the late eighth century, which is the root of the argument in section 06.

items.name: The copper works of Faynan
items.what: Khirbat en-Nahas and other smelting sites in the Faynan district, at the edge of the Arabah, excavated by Thomas E. Levy, Mohammad Najjar, Erez Ben-Yosef and others.
items.kept: The sites are in southern Jordan.
items.date: Major smelting in the tenth and ninth centuries BC, by high-precision radiocarbon dates published in 2008.
items.evidence: Khirbat en-Nahas was the largest copper production centre of its time in the southern Levant, with a fortress and workshops.
items.inference: Someone organised copper production on a large scale in Edom's lowlands two centuries before Bozrah's buildings. Who, and whether it was a kingdom, is section 06.
items.limit: No inscription at Faynan names Edom. The excavators call the producers Edomite from the place.

items.name: Horvat Qitmit, an Edomite shrine in Judah's Negev
items.what: A shrine found in a survey in 1979 and excavated in 1984-1986 by Itzhaq Beit-Arieh, with Edomite pottery and clay figures, and three incomplete inscriptions with the name Qos.
items.kept: Finds with the Israel Antiquities Authority (not confirmed in the sources read).
items.date: The late seventh and early sixth centuries BC.
items.evidence: Edomites worshipped Qos inside the land Judah held, in Judah's last decades.
items.inference: It matches Scripture's Edom pressing on Judah's south when Jerusalem fell (section 07, step 12).
items.limit: Whether the shrine served settlers, traders or raiders is argued.

items.name: A letter from Arad: "lest Edom should come there"
items.what: A Hebrew letter on a potsherd (Arad ostracon 24), sent to the commander of Judah's fort at Arad, ordering men to Ramat-Negeb lest Edom come there.
items.kept: The Israel Museum, Jerusalem (not confirmed in the sources read).
items.date: About 600 BC, from the fort's last level before Jerusalem's fall.
items.evidence: Judah's own officers feared an Edomite attack in its southern desert.
items.inference: Psalm 137:7 and Obadiah remember Edom's part in Judah's fall; Arad shows the fear of it beforehand, in Judah's own hand.
items.limit: The letter names no battle, and does not say that Edom came.

items.name: "Shasu of Edom" in an Egyptian report
items.what: A frontier official's report in Papyrus Anastasi VI, saying that the Shasu tribes of Edom had been let past a fortress of Merneptah in the eastern Delta to the pools, to keep themselves and their herds alive.
items.kept: The British Museum (not confirmed in the sources read).
items.date: The end of the thirteenth century BC.
items.evidence: Egypt knew Edom by name, as the home of herding tribes, around 1200 BC.
items.inference: Edom was a recognised people and land before any of its kings is named outside Scripture, as Genesis 36 implies.
items.limit: "Shasu" is Egypt's word for herders of the southern steppe; the report says nothing of kings.

items.name: A king's sealing from Umm el-Biyara
items.what: A clay sealing from Crystal-M. Bennett's excavations of 1960-1965 on the mountain of Umm el-Biyara at Petra, reading Qos-ga[br], king of E[dom], with letters partly restored.
items.kept: Not confirmed in the sources read.
items.date: The seventh century BC, by the king's name, which Esarhaddon's list gives for 676-673 BC.
items.evidence: An Edomite king named Qaus-gabri in Assyria's records sealed goods in Edom with his own name.
items.inference: One Edomite king is known from both an Assyrian list and his own seal. Scripture does not name him.
items.limit: The end of the name and the word Edom are restored, and the sealing was not found in a sealed layer.

items.name: Balaam son of Beor on a plaster wall at Deir Alla
items.what: Ink writing in black and red on wall plaster, found in 1967 at Tell Deir Alla in the Jordan valley, surviving in 119 fragments. It tells of a vision of "Balaam son of Beor", a seer of the gods.
items.kept: Not confirmed in the sources read.
items.date: About 825 BC is often given; the range proposed runs from about 880 to 770 BC.
items.evidence: A seer named Balaam son of Beor was remembered east of the Jordan, in the land between Ammon and Israel, centuries after Numbers sets him.
items.inference: Numbers 22 to 24 and the plaster text name the same figure, in the same part of the world. The plaster text is a different story about him, not an account of Balak's commission.
items.limit: Its language is disputed, a dialect some call Aramaic and others a local Canaanite tongue, and its fragments have been pieced together in more than one way. It is placed with Ammon here only by geography.

stories.lead: Scripture ties the three to Israel by birth before it sets them against Israel in war. Read in order, the passages move between kinship, refusal, war, marriage and judgment, and never let go of the kinship.

steps.title: Lot's sons
steps.evidence: Moab and Ben-ammi are born to Lot's daughters by their father, and each is named "the father of the Moabites of today" and "of the Ammonites of today" (Genesis 19:37-38 · BSB).
steps.inference: Genesis gives the two peoples a shameful beginning and a real one: they are Abraham's nephew's descendants, kin to Israel.
steps.limit: Whether the story is told to shame Israel's rivals is read differently; the text reports it without comment.

steps.title: Esau, who is Edom
steps.evidence: Esau sells his birthright for red stew, "That is why he was also called Edom" (Genesis 25:30 · BSB); Isaac tells him, "you will tear his yoke from your neck" (Genesis 27:40 · BSB); the brothers meet, and "they both wept" (Genesis 33:4 · BSB). Genesis 36 lists "the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites" (Genesis 36:31 · BSB).
steps.inference: The twins' story is the pattern for the two nations: rivalry, service, rebellion, and a reconciliation that does not last.
steps.limit: Genesis 36's kings are not named in any outside record, and their dates are not given. Section 06 takes up what that list can and cannot show.

steps.title: Lands Israel was not to take
steps.evidence: To each the LORD says the same: "I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession" (Deuteronomy 2:5 · BSB); Ar "to the descendants of Lot" (Deuteronomy 2:9 · BSB); Ammon's land "to the descendants of Lot as their possession" (Deuteronomy 2:19 · BSB).
steps.inference: The three kingdoms' land is the LORD's gift to them, as Canaan is to Israel. Scripture's God rules the nations' borders, not Israel's alone.
steps.limit: This is Deuteronomy's account of the march; it does not say when the kingdoms first became kingdoms.

steps.title: Passage refused, a prophet hired
steps.evidence: Moses' message to Edom begins, "This is what your brother Israel says" (Numbers 20:14 · BSB), and "Edom refused to allow Israel to pass" (Numbers 20:21 · BSB). "Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab at that time" (Numbers 22:4 · BSB) and hires Balaam, whose last oracles see "A star will come forth from Jacob" that "will crush the skulls of Moab" (Numbers 24:17 · BSB). At Shittim the men of Israel turn to "the daughters of Moab" (Numbers 25:1 · BSB) and their god.
steps.inference: Numbers 20 to 25 sets out every later quarrel in small: Edom's refusal, Moab's fear, a curse turned to blessing, and the pull of Moab's worship.
steps.limit: An inscription from Deir Alla in the Jordan valley names a seer called Balaam son of Beor (section 05). It shows such a figure was remembered east of the Jordan; it is not an account of Numbers 22 to 24.

steps.title: The assembly, and a brother
steps.evidence: "No Ammonite or Moabite ... may enter the assembly of the LORD, even to the tenth generation" (Deuteronomy 23:3 · BSB), because they did not meet Israel "with food and water" and hired Balaam (Deuteronomy 23:4 · BSB). But "Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7 · BSB).
steps.inference: The law treats the three differently, and gives its reasons from the wilderness years. Edom, which refused passage, is still called brother.
steps.limit: How this law sits with Ruth (step 07) has been read in several ways since ancient times; the Mishnah, for one, applies it to men and not to women (Yevamot 8:3, named from this study's knowledge, not read for this draft). Nehemiah applies it to the community of his day (Nehemiah 13:1).

steps.title: Oppressors and deliverers
steps.evidence: The LORD "gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel" (Judges 3:12 · BSB) until Ehud. The king of the Ammonites claims land "from the Arnon to the Jabbok" (Judges 11:13 · BSB) and Jephthah answers him with history. "Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead" (1 Samuel 11:1 · BSB), and Saul's first act as king is to save it.
steps.inference: In Judges and early Samuel, Moab and Ammon are the LORD's means of discipline, and Israel's first king is made in a war with Ammon.
steps.limit: No outside record names Eglon or Nahash.

steps.title: Ruth the Moabite
steps.evidence: Ruth tells Naomi, "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16 · BSB). Her son Obed "became the father of Jesse, the father of David" (Ruth 4:17 · BSB), and Matthew names her in Jesus' line: "Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth" (Matthew 1:5 · BSB).
steps.inference: David's great-grandmother was a Moabite who took Israel's God as her own. A Moabite stands in the line of the Messiah.
steps.limit: The book is read here for this fact only. Its story is the Theological studies' to tell.

steps.title: David's refuge and David's wars
steps.evidence: A fugitive, David asks the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother stay with you" (1 Samuel 22:3 · BSB). As king he subdues Moab, so that "the Moabites became subject to David and brought him tribute" (2 Samuel 8:2 · BSB), and "He placed garrisons throughout Edom" (2 Samuel 8:14 · BSB). He says, "I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash" (2 Samuel 10:2 · BSB), but his envoys are shamed, and takes Rabbah. Later, fleeing Absalom, he is fed by "Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites" (2 Samuel 17:27 · BSB).
steps.inference: David's dealings with all three are both kin and conquest, in the same reign. The books keep the kindness beside the war.
steps.limit: No inscription names David's wars in the east. How large a realm "garrisons throughout Edom" implies is part of the argument in section 06.

steps.title: Solomon's wives and their gods
steps.evidence: Solomon loved "women of Moab, Ammon, Edom, and Sidon" (1 Kings 11:1 · BSB) and built high places for Chemosh and Molech; "the LORD raised up against Solomon an adversary, Hadad the Edomite" (1 Kings 11:14 · BSB). Rehoboam, the next king of Judah, was the son of "Naamah the Ammonite" (1 Kings 14:21 · BSB).
steps.inference: Every later king of David's line descended from Naamah the Ammonite, as David himself descended from Ruth the Moabite. Kings presents the marriages as the door the neighbours' gods came through.
steps.limit: The high places east of Jerusalem have not been found.

steps.title: Mesha's revolt
steps.evidence: "After the death of Ahab, Moab rebelled against Israel" (2 Kings 1:1 · BSB). Israel, Judah and "the king of Edom" march round the Dead Sea (2 Kings 3:9 · BSB). Besieged, Mesha tries "to break through to the king of Edom" (2 Kings 3:26 · BSB), then offers his firstborn son "as a burnt offering on the city wall. And there was great fury against the Israelites, so they withdrew" (2 Kings 3:27 · BSB).
steps.inference: Edom is Israel's ally here, yet Mesha aims his break-out at Edom's king: perhaps the weakest point of the line, perhaps an ally he hoped would change sides. The text does not say which.
steps.limit: Whose "fury" fell on Israel is not said: Moab's, roused by the sacrifice; Israel's own horror; or, as some read it, divine wrath. The comparison of the chapter with the stele is in From discovery to history.

steps.title: Edom breaks away
steps.evidence: Under Jehoshaphat "there was no king in Edom; a deputy served as king" (1 Kings 22:47 · BSB). Under his son, "Edom rebelled against the hand of Judah and appointed their own king" (2 Kings 8:20 · BSB). Amaziah later "struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt" and took Sela (2 Kings 14:7 · BSB).
steps.inference: Isaac's word, "you will tear his yoke from your neck" (Genesis 27:40 · BSB), is fulfilled in Kings in the ordinary language of revolt.
steps.limit: These events have no outside record; the first Edomite king named outside Scripture appears in Assyrian lists about a century later (section 02).

steps.title: When Jerusalem fell
steps.evidence: Moabite and Ammonite raiders are sent against Jehoiakim (2 Kings 24:2). Zedekiah hosts envoys from "the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon" (Jeremiah 27:3 · BSB). After the fall, "Baalis king of the Ammonites" sends a man to kill Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:14 · BSB), and the psalm remembers "the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell" (Psalm 137:7 · BSB).
steps.inference: In Judah's last years the three are by turns raiders, fellow plotters against Babylon, and gloating neighbours. Edom's part on the day itself is what the prophets never forgive (section 08).
steps.limit: No outside text describes Edom's part on the day the city fell. A seal impression naming a servant of Ba'alyasha, probably Baalis, is the one outside witness to these people; a letter from Arad shows Judah fearing Edom in the same years (section 05).

steps.title: After the return
steps.evidence: "Tobiah the Ammonite official" opposes Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:10 · BSB), and the law that "no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God" is read aloud and applied (Nehemiah 13:1 · BSB).
steps.inference: By the Persian period the old kingdoms are gone, but the names remain, attached to people and to a law.
steps.limit: Tobiah is the opponent the draft Cyrus, restoration and return treats; here he closes the Old Testament's line of Ammonites.

oracles.lead: Five prophets speak to the three neighbours by name. Set side by side, their charges are about what each did to others, and their endings differ.

rows.edom: "he pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion" (Amos 1:11 · BSB)
rows.ammon: "they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory" (Amos 1:13 · BSB)
rows.moab: "he burned to lime the bones of Edom’s king" (Amos 2:1 · BSB)
rows.hope: None for the three in these oracles. Amos ends with David's line restored, "that they may possess the remnant of Edom" (Amos 9:12 · BSB).

rows.edom: "the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom" (Isaiah 34:6 · BSB)
rows.moab: "Ar in Moab is ruined, destroyed in a night!" (Isaiah 15:1 · BSB), a lament more than a charge: "Dibon goes up to its temple to weep" (Isaiah 15:2 · BSB).
rows.hope: Inside the Moab oracle: "a throne will be established in the tent of David" (Isaiah 16:5 · BSB).

rows.edom: "Is there no longer wisdom in Teman?" (Jeremiah 49:7 · BSB); "Bozrah will become a desolation" (Jeremiah 49:13 · BSB)
rows.ammon: "Why then has Milcom taken possession of Gad?" (Jeremiah 49:1 · BSB)
rows.moab: "Because you trust in your works and treasures" (Jeremiah 48:7 · BSB); Moab "will be ashamed of Chemosh" (Jeremiah 48:13 · BSB)
rows.hope: Moab: "Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity" (Jeremiah 48:47 · BSB). Ammon: "Yet afterward I will restore the Ammonites from captivity" (Jeremiah 49:6 · BSB). Edom: no such line.

rows.edom: "Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah" (Ezekiel 25:12 · BSB)
rows.ammon: "you exclaimed, “Aha!” when My sanctuary was profaned" (Ezekiel 25:3 · BSB)
rows.moab: "Moab and Seir said, “Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations,”" (Ezekiel 25:8 · BSB)
rows.hope: None. Each oracle ends with the nation coming to know the LORD, or his vengeance.

rows.edom: "The pride of your heart has deceived you" (Obadiah 1:3 · BSB); "Because of the violence against your brother Jacob" (Obadiah 1:10 · BSB); "you should not gloat in that day, your brother’s day of misfortune" (Obadiah 1:12 · BSB)
rows.hope: "The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD" (Obadiah 1:21 · BSB).

oracles.evidence: Amos's charge against Moab is a wrong done to Edom, not to Israel. Ezekiel's charges are words of contempt spoken when Judah fell. Jeremiah closes the oracles on Moab and Ammon with a promise of restoration and gives Edom none; Obadiah, the shortest book of the Old Testament, is about Edom alone.
oracles.inference: The LORD judges the neighbours for cruelty to anyone, and most of all for cruelty to a brother in his ruin. Edom, the nearest kin, carries the heaviest sentence, and becomes in Isaiah and Obadiah a name for every nation that sets itself against the LORD's people.
oracles.limit: Which events each oracle answers is argued, above all for Obadiah, whose date is not given; most readers set it after Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC, some earlier. When James quotes Amos 9:12 at the council in Jerusalem, the words read "so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord" (Acts 15:17 · BSB), where the Berean's Amos has "the remnant of Edom". The usual explanation is that James's wording follows the Greek translation of Amos, which read the Hebrew letters differently; it is to be checked against a named commentary before a page states it.

idumeans.head: From Edom to Idumea
idumeans.lead: Edom's name outlived its kingdom. By the time of the New Testament it belonged to a district of southern Judea, and to the family of Herod.

steps.title: Edomites west of the Arabah
steps.evidence: Late in Judah's monarchy Edomite pottery and a shrine with inscriptions to Qos appear in the Negev at Horvat Qitmit, south of Hebron's hills, dated to the late seventh and early sixth centuries BC. An ostracon from Arad warns of Edom.
steps.inference: Edomites were moving into Judah's southern lands in the years Obadiah and Psalm 137 remember.
steps.limit: Whether they came as settlers, traders or raiders, and how many, is argued.

steps.title: Idumea
steps.evidence: The Greek form of Edom's name is Idumea. In Persian and Greek times it named the land around Hebron, south of the province of Judah, where Edomites and others now lived.
steps.inference: The old kingdom east of the Arabah had passed to other peoples, the Nabataeans among them; its name moved west with the Edomites.
steps.limit: How and when the eastern kingdom ended is not recorded; Babylonian campaigns of the sixth century are usually thought to have ended it.

steps.title: Made Jews by force
steps.evidence: Josephus, writing in the first century AD, says that John Hyrcanus, the Jewish high priest and ruler, "subdued all the Idumeans; and permitted them to stay in that countrey, if they would circumcise their genitals, and make use of the laws of the Jews" (Antiquities 13.9.1, in Whiston's translation of 1737).
steps.inference: From then on the Idumeans counted as Jews, though some Jews still saw them as outsiders.
steps.limit: Josephus gives no year here, and modern dates for the conquest run from about 128 to about 112 BC. His account is the main one.

steps.title: Herod's family
steps.evidence: Josephus names Herod's father as "an Idumean, called Antipater" (Antiquities 14.1.3), and has Antigonus, Herod's rival, protest that Herod was "no more than a private man, and an Idumean, i. e. an half Jew" (Antiquities 14.15.2, both in Whiston's translation).
steps.inference: Herod the Great, king of Judea when Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1), came of an Idumean family that had been Jewish for two or three generations. A family from the land that kept Edom's name ruled the land of Jacob.
steps.limit: The New Testament never calls Herod an Idumean; that comes from Josephus. Even in antiquity it was disputed: Josephus reports that Herod's court historian, Nicolaus of Damascus, traced Antipater to the leading Jews who came back from Babylon, and says Nicolaus wrote that to flatter Herod.

steps.title: Idumea in the Gospels
steps.evidence: Crowds come to Jesus from "Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon" (Mark 3:8 · BSB). It is the one time the New Testament names Idumea.
steps.inference: People from Edom's old name came to hear Jesus with Judeans and Galileans. Mark lists them without comment.
steps.limit: Who they were, Idumean Jews or others living there, is not said.

steps.title: Esau in the New Testament
steps.evidence: Paul quotes Malachi: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated" (Romans 9:13 · BSB). Hebrews warns against being "godless like Esau, who for a single meal sold his birthright" (Hebrews 12:16 · BSB).
steps.inference: In the New Testament Esau appears as a person and an example, not as a nation. The Edomites of Herod's day are not discussed.
steps.limit: What Romans 9 teaches about God's choosing is a theological question, read differently among Christians and among Baptists; it is the Theological studies' to show, not this one's.

explanations.name: A late kingdom
explanations.tag: Edom became a kingdom only under Assyria, from the late eighth century BC
explanations.held: Piotr Bienkowski, editor of the final report on Bozrah, and many archaeologists of Jordan; Israel Finkelstein has argued the same from the dating of settlements (his papers located, not read).
explanations.forIt: Bozrah's large buildings and most of Edom's highland villages date from the late eighth century BC on; the first Edomite kings named outside Scripture appear in Assyrian lists from about 733 BC.
explanations.against: It reads absence of buildings as absence of rule, and must set aside the copper works of Faynan, which were run on a large scale centuries earlier.
explanations.wouldShow: Proof that Faynan's tenth-century industry was run by people who were not Edom's ancestors, or by an outside power.

explanations.name: An early kingdom without palaces
explanations.tag: A mostly tent-dwelling society ran an organised copper industry in the tenth century BC
explanations.held: Thomas E. Levy, Erez Ben-Yosef and their colleagues, from radiocarbon dates at Khirbat en-Nahas in Faynan (2008), and Ben-Yosef's argument against an "architectural bias" in the field (2019).
explanations.forIt: Radiocarbon dates put large-scale copper smelting at Faynan in the tenth and ninth centuries BC, with a fortress and workshops; producing and trading copper on that scale needs organisation, whether or not its people built stone houses.
explanations.against: No inscription from Faynan names Edom, so calling its people Edomites is an inference from place. Others accept the dates but doubt that a centralised kingdom stood behind them.
explanations.wouldShow: A tenth-century text or seal naming Edom or an Edomite ruler from the Faynan district.

explanationsNote.head: Kings before Israel had kings? The text and the spade
explanationsNote.evidence: Genesis lists kings of Edom "before any king reigned over the Israelites" (Genesis 36:31 · BSB), next to its "chiefs of Edom" (Genesis 36:43 · BSB). Exodus's song names "the chiefs of Edom" and "the leaders of Moab" (Exodus 15:15 · BSB). David places "garrisons throughout Edom" (2 Samuel 8:14 · BSB).
explanationsNote.inference: Scripture's early Edom is a land of clan chiefs and of kings who do not pass the throne from father to son, a picture that fits a people who need not have built palaces. The text does not need Bozrah's buildings to be early, and the spade has not yet shown whether they were.
explanationsNote.limit: The site does not choose between the two explanations. Either is consistent with Genesis 36, which gives no dates; neither proves it.

rows.name: "Shasu of Edom" in an Egyptian report (Papyrus Anastasi VI)
rows.note: Late thirteenth or about 1200 BC; the papyrus's own date is a king's year, converted.

rows.name: David's reign
rows.note: The usual dates, reckoned from the books of Kings; they are not written in the text.

rows.name: Copper smelting at Khirbat en-Nahas, Faynan
rows.note: The tenth and ninth centuries BC by radiocarbon (Levy and others, 2008). Drawn faint: its ends are not measured to the year.

rows.name: Ahab dies; Moab rebels (2 Kings 1:1)
rows.note: The usual date of Ahab's death, 853 or 852 BC.

rows.name: The Mesha Stele set up
rows.note: A range: the Louvre's catalogue gives about 830-805 BC, other discussions earlier, as From discovery to history reports. Never a point.

rows.name: The Amman Citadel inscription
rows.note: The later ninth century BC, by the shape of its letters. An estimate.

rows.name: Tiglath-pileser III's tribute list names kings of Ammon, Moab and Edom
rows.note: About 733 BC.

rows.name: Bozrah's main buildings in use
rows.note: From the late eighth century into the sixth, as the final report dates them. Drawn faint at both ends.

rows.name: Sennacherib's annals name kings of the three
rows.note: 701 BC, the campaign of 2 Kings 18-19.

rows.name: Esarhaddon's list of 22 kings
rows.note: As the prism is usually dated.

rows.name: The Tell Siran bottle
rows.note: About 600 BC by Frank Moore Cross's dating of the letters; its first editors placed it earlier in the seventh century. A range.

rows.name: The Edomite shrine at Horvat Qitmit
rows.note: The late seventh and early sixth centuries BC, as the excavators date it.

rows.name: Jerusalem falls; Baalis and Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:14)
rows.note: 586 BC, as usually converted; some reckon 587.

rows.name: John Hyrcanus conquers Idumea
rows.note: Josephus gives no year; modern dates run from about 128 to about 112 BC. Drawn as a range, not a point.

rows.name: Herod the Great, king of Judea
rows.note: 37 to 4 BC, the usual dates.

timeline.undated: Lot's sons, Esau, the kings of Genesis 36, the wilderness years, Eglon and Ruth carry no date in the text that can be converted without argument, so they have no bar. The oracles of Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel sit in their prophets' dated careers; Obadiah's date is not given.

stance.head: What this site holds
stance.confessionSource: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, on Scripture
stance.body: The site reads every passage in this study as Scripture, and holds that it tells the truth. Mesha's stele, the Ammonite inscriptions and the Assyrian lists are evidence about the world Scripture describes, reported for what they show; they do not prove it, and where they are silent or damaged they do not overturn it. Scripture's own picture of the three neighbours is not flattering to Israel or to them. It says the LORD gave them their land as he gave Israel its land: "I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession" (Deuteronomy 2:19 · BSB). It judges them for cruelty to anyone, and most of all for cruelty to a brother. It puts a Moabite woman in the line of David and of Christ, and promises Moab and Ammon restoration. Their gods are named as gods that failed; their peoples are named as people the LORD rules, judges and does not forget.

claims.claim: “Moab, Ammon and Edom were simply Israel's enemies.”
claims.head: Enemies, often. Kin, always.
claims.evidence: They fight Israel from Numbers to Nehemiah. But Deuteronomy forbids Israel to take their land, calls the Edomite "your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7 · BSB), and Scripture records a king of Moab sheltering David's parents, an Ammonite prince feeding David in flight, Ruth the Moabite, and Naamah the Ammonite, mother of Judah's kings.
claims.inference: Scripture keeps kinship and enmity in the same story, and judges the neighbours as kin who should have known better.
claims.limit: This is Scripture's own picture. The neighbours' few texts say almost nothing of Israel except, on Mesha's stele, as an enemy.

test.question: Deuteronomy 2:19 tells Israel not to provoke the Ammonites. What reason does it give?

options.text: Ammon was too strong to attack.
options.why: Numbers 21:24 does say Ammon's border was fortified, but Deuteronomy 2:19 gives a different reason.

options.text: The LORD had given Ammon's land to the descendants of Lot.
options.why: That is the verse's own reason: "I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession" (Deuteronomy 2:19 · BSB).

options.text: Israel had made a treaty with Ammon.
options.why: No treaty is mentioned. The reason is the LORD's gift of the land.

claims.claim: “Edom had no kingdom until the Assyrians came.”
claims.head: No palace found. Not proof of no rule.
claims.evidence: Bozrah's large buildings date from the late eighth century BC on. But radiocarbon dates put an organised copper industry at Faynan, in Edom's lowlands, in the tenth and ninth centuries BC (Levy and others, 2008), and Ben-Yosef argues that a largely tent-dwelling society can still be ruled.
claims.inference: Absence of stone palaces is evidence about building, not proof about government. The question is open, and the two explanations above give each side.
claims.limit: No early inscription names Edom at Faynan; calling its copper-workers Edomites is an inference from place.

test.question: No tenth-century palace has been found in Edom's highlands. What may you conclude?

options.text: That Edom had no ruler in the tenth century.
options.why: A ruler need not build a palace, and Faynan's copper works point to organisation at that date.

options.text: That nothing in the highlands shows a tenth-century state, and other evidence must be weighed.
options.why: This is what an absence can carry. The copper works are the other evidence.
Genesis 36 gives no dates, and no find names its kings.

claims.claim: “The New Testament says Herod was an Edomite.”
claims.head: Josephus says it. The Gospels do not.
claims.evidence: Matthew, Luke and Acts name Herod and his family as kings and tetrarchs, and never their descent. Josephus, writing in the first century AD, says Herod's father Antipater was an Idumean, and that a rival called Herod an Idumean and a half-Jew.
claims.inference: Herod's Idumean family is well attested, but by a historian, not by Scripture. Sermons that read Herod as Esau's heir are drawing on Josephus.
claims.limit: Josephus is read here in Whiston's public-domain translation of 1737, on the LacusCurtius site. Nicolaus of Damascus, Herod's own historian, gave Herod's family a Jewish descent from the exiles; Josephus calls that flattery.

test.question: Where is Idumea named in the New Testament?

options.why: Matthew 2 names Herod as king, not where his family came from.

options.text: In Mark 3:8, in a list of places the crowds came from.
options.why: It is the one place the New Testament uses the name.

claims.claim: “Inscriptions from Israel's neighbours exist to confirm the Bible.”
claims.head: Seldom confirmation. Mostly a wider world.
claims.evidence: Of the neighbours' kings named outside Scripture, only Mesha certainly, and Baalis probably, are also named in it. The Tell Siran bottle names three Ammonite kings, Amminadab, Hissalel and Amminadab, whom Scripture never mentions. Qos, Edom's god, is known only from outside it.
claims.inference: Such finds mainly widen the picture: more kings, a god's name, the land's industry. Where they touch Scripture, as Mesha does, they show the same world from the other side.
claims.limit: This is a count of what has been found and published. New finds can change it.

test.question: The Tell Siran bottle names Amminadab, king of the Ammonites. Which king in Scripture is he?

options.why: That Amminadab is an ancestor of David in Judah, centuries earlier. The name is shared.

options.text: None: Scripture does not name him.
options.why: The bottle adds a king, and his father and grandfather, to what is known. It neither confirms nor contradicts Scripture.
Nahash lived in Saul's and David's day, about four centuries before the bottle.

confusedWords.word: Edom, Seir, Esau, Teman and Idumea
confusedWords.note: Edom is the people and land; Seir is its mountain country; Esau is its ancestor, and his name stands for the nation in Obadiah and Malachi; Teman is a clan and region often used for the whole; Idumea is the Greek form of Edom, used in later times for the land around Hebron.
Ammon is the people and kingdom; Rabbah, "Rabbah of the Ammonites" (2 Samuel 12:26 · BSB), its capital; Amman, the modern city on the same site and the capital of Jordan.

Milcom is the Ammonite god's name, in Scripture and in Ammon's inscriptions. Molech is a related name, tied to Ammon once (1 Kings 11:7) and elsewhere to child sacrifice; whether it is the same god is argued. The Hebrew for "their king" is close to Milcom in spelling.

confusedWords.word: Kir-hareseth, Kir-haraseth, Kir-heres and Kir in Moab
confusedWords.note: The Berean's spellings of what most readers take as one Moabite city, usually identified with Kerak: 2 Kings 3:25, Isaiah 16:7, Jeremiah 48:31 and Isaiah 15:1.

confusedWords.word: Bozrah in Edom and Bozrah in Moab
confusedWords.note: Edom's Bozrah is Buseirah (Jeremiah 49:13). Jeremiah 48:24 names a Bozrah among "all the towns of Moab" (Jeremiah 48:24 · BSB), a different place.
Two names for one object, Louvre AO 5066.

confusedWords.word: House of David and City of David
confusedWords.note: "House of David" means David's dynasty, the reading proposed for line 31 of the stele. The City of David is a place, the oldest part of Jerusalem.
A people or town given wholly to a god by being destroyed. Scripture uses it of Israel's wars (Joshua 6:17); Mesha uses the same idea for Chemosh. Same practice, different gods.
In Numbers, the road Israel asked to use. Today, the name of the old route through Jordan's highlands, taken from Numbers. The modern road need not follow the ancient one exactly.

The three gorges that served as borders: the Arnon (Wadi Mujib) between Moab's heartland and the tableland to its north, the Zered (Wadi Hasa) between Moab and Edom, the Jabbok (Wadi Zarqa) along Ammon's land. The Berean calls the second "the Brook of Zered" (Deuteronomy 2:13 · BSB).
An Ammonite king of the seventh century BC, on the Tell Siran bottle; and David's ancestor in Judah, in Ruth 4:19. One name, two men.

reach: Scripture is read whole for the three neighbours: the passages in the stories and oracles sections, chosen because they name Moab, Ammon, Edom, Seir or their kings, not every verse that mentions them. This is a selection, not a census.

Objects are a selection too: the inscriptions and sites that name a god or a king, or that the scholarly argument turns on. Many Ammonite and Edomite seals, and the excavations at Ammonite and Moabite towns, are left out.
The Mesha Stele's object record, its comparison with 2 Kings 3, and the full argument over line 31 are left to From discovery to history and linked, by the owner's scope of 2026-11-05.

Several facts are reported through Wikipedia or search results rather than read in the scholars' own publications; the reading trail says which. Assyrian royal names are spelled as the named translations give them.
That Mark 3:8 is the only verse in the New Testament naming Idumea was checked by script against the site's whole Berean text.
Every verse and phrase from Scripture in this file is checked by script against the site's Berean text. That proves the words are there, not that a reading of them is right.
